# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall series.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall series)
B1. Non-detained docket: house line is "13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities" (ICE data).
B2. Federal sentencing: use the all-offense share, "more than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences". The fall series does not break out offense type.
B3. Approved sources for the fall series: ICE, USSC, GAO, Texas DPS, CIS.
B4. Source line for B1-B3 figures: "Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)".
B5. Appendix notes: source line only.
B6. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B4 for B1-B3; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

HTTP 200
Trump, Vance Wrong About 'Illegal Immigrant Murderers' - FactCheck.org 

 Skip to main content 

 FactCheck .org ® 

 A Project of The Annenberg Public Policy Center 

 This article is available in both English and Español 
 English 
 Español 

 In campaign appearances over the weekend in the swing state of Pennsylvania, former President Donald Trump and his running mate, Sen. JD Vance, falsely accused Vice President Kamala Harris of letting more than 13,000 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States.

 It’s true that there were 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder, as of July 21, who were not being detained by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 

 But the “vast majority” of them entered the country prior to the Biden administration and had their custody status determined “long before this Administration,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement, noting that many were in prison. Also, the noncitizens include those who entered the country legally, such as green-card holders.

 Trump and Vance distorted the contents of a Sept. 25 letter that Patrick Lechleitner , the acting director of ICE, sent to Rep. Tony Gonzales . The Republican congressman had requested the number of noncitizens who had committed a crime but were not in ICE custody — a list known as the agency’s non-detained docket.

 Lechleitner’s response included a chart that showed there are 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder who were not being detained by ICE. Homeland Security later clarified in its statement that “many” are in prisons, although it did not tell us how many are incarcerated when we inquired.

 Gonzales posted Lechleitner’s letter to X on Sept. 27. The next day, Vance referenced the 13,099 murderers at a campaign event in Newtown, Pennsylvania , and Trump did the same in Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin . A day later, Trump repeated the claim in Erie, Pennsylvania .

 Vance, Sept. 28: Do you know that there are 13,000 — I know some of you are nodding because some of you saw this — 13,000 illegal immigrant murderers in the United States of America right now. They’re in this country because Kamala Harris let them in this country. 

 Trump, Sept. 29: During her term, it’s not even believable, she let in 13,099 convicted murderers. Some of them had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven. One murdered six.

 In its statement, the Department of Homeland Security said data in Lechleitner’s letter had been “misinterpreted.”

 “The data goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this Administration,” the statement said. “It also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners.”

 Similarly, Michelle Mittelstadt , director of communications for the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute, told us that people have been on the non-detained docket “for decades.”

 “There is a lot of confusion around the non-detained docket,” including “who is on it and how long they’ve been on it,” Mittelstadt said in an email. “This docket has grown under multiple administrations, including the Trump one. Significant numbers of people on the docket have been on it for decades.”

 For example, the ICE acting director said in his letter that there are 425,431 convicted criminals on the agency’s non-detained docket as of July 21. But, as Mittelstadt noted, ICE reported in a budget document “that there were 405,786 convicted criminal noncitizens on the non-detained docket in June 2021 – so the vast majority would have gotten on during the prior administrations as the Biden administration by then was just five months old.” The number of people on the docket has increased by nearly 5% in about three years.

 She also told us that “the non-detained docket includes not just unauthorized immigrants but green-card holders and noncitizens on long-term non-immigrant visas who have made themselves removable by virtue of a criminal conviction.”

 The ICE letter to Gonzales did show that, as of July 21, there were an additional 1,845 noncitizens on the non-detained docket who face murder charges. But, again, we don’t know when those 1,845 people entered the United States, how many of them may have entered illegally and when they committed their alleged crimes. We also do not know if they are being held by other local, state or federal law enforcement agencies. A Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond when we asked for such information.

 We asked the Trump campaign to respond to the evidence that contradicts its candidates’ claims that Harris let 13,099 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States. We also asked it to supply information about Trump’s claim that some of the 13,099 “had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven.” In response, Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s national press secretary, said Trump “will begin the largest mass deportation in history on day one.”

 Mittelstadt said some murderers and other criminals cannot be deported “because their country will not accept their return.” In addition, she said, a 2001 Supreme Court ruling generally bars ICE from detaining noncitizens for more than six months if they are unlikely to be deported. As a result, ICE says on its website that it “has been legally required to release thousands of noncitizens, including those with serious criminal convictions.”

 Editor’s note: FactCheck.org does not accept advertising. We rely on grants and individual donations from people like you. Please consider a donation. Credit card donations may be made through  our “Donate” page . If you prefer to give by check, send to: FactCheck.org, Annenberg Public Policy Center, P.O. Box 58100, Philadelphia, PA 19102.  

 Ask FactCheck 
 Q: Claims about James Talarico being hospitalized in a mental health facility. Is this true? 

 A: No. An Ohio mental health center rebutted false online rumors that Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, had been there as a patient. Talarico said he was off the campaign trail for several days in early October while recovering from the flu at his Texas home. 

 Read the full question and answer View the Ask FactCheck archives Have a question? Ask us.

 Delegation of Immigration Authority Section 287(g) Immigration and Nationality Act

 ICE’s 287(g) Program
 The Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 added Section 287(g) to the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), authorizing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to delegate state and local law enforcement officers the authority to perform specified immigration officer functions under ICE’s direction and oversight.
 The Program enhances the safety and security of our nation’s communities by allowing ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) to partner with state, local, and tribal law enforcement agencies to identify and remove criminal aliens who are amenable to removal from the United States.
 ICE recognizes the importance of its relationships with law enforcement partners—including state and local agencies—to carry out its critical mission.
 Through the delegation of specified immigration officer duties, the program allows ICE to enhance collaboration with state and local law enforcement partners to protect the homeland through the arrest and removal of aliens who undermine the safety of our nation’s communities and the integrity of U.S. immigration laws.
 What’s in It for Your Law Enforcement Agency?
 The 287(g) Program benefits state and local law enforcement agencies in several ways — but most notably, it helps you keep your community safe from potentially dangerous criminal aliens. Your law enforcement officers will get access to ICE resources and training. ICE covers the cost of training (see the later section, “287(g) Training Available to State and Local Law Enforcement,” for more information).
 Your agency or office may be eligible for the Department of Justice’s State Criminal Alien Assistance Program . This Department of Justice program administers SCAAP awards and provides federal funding to states and political subdivisions of states, including municipalities that incur costs for incarcerating certain criminal aliens. This is entirely separate from the 287(g) program. 
 ICE 287(g) Program Map

 287(g) Program Models
 ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations operates three 287(g) models:
 The  Jail Enforcement Model allows designated immigration officers to identify and process removable aliens who have pending or active criminal charges.
 The  Task Force Model  enhances public safety and national security by allowing designated immigration officers to enforce limited immigration authority while performing routine police duties or as an active participant in an ICE-led task force.
 The Warrant Service Officer Model allows designated immigration officers to serve and execute administrative warrants on aliens in their custody.
 How Can Your Agency Participate in the ICE 287(g) Program?
 On January 20, 2025, President Donald J. Trump issued Executive Order (EO) 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion . This EO requires ICE to authorize State and local law enforcement officials, as the Secretary of Homeland Security determines are qualified and appropriate, under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act to the maximum extent permitted by law. Several states, including but not limited to Georgia and Florida, have passed, or are considering, State legislation mandating law enforcement agencies (LEAs) seek out or enter into memorandums of agreement (MOA) with ICE pursuant to a partnership under the 287(g) Program.
 Participation in the 287(g) Program is limited to LEAs only. LEAs interested in participating in the 287(g) Program must sign an MOA with ICE. LEAs will nominate officers to participate in the 287(g) Program. Nominees must possess U.S. citizenship, complete and pass a background investigation, and have knowledge of and have enforced laws and regulations related to law enforcement activities at their jurisdictions. Task Force Model nominees must also have at least two (2) years of total law enforcement officer experience. Nominees will receive training at the expense of ICE related to the immigration duties pertinent to the applicable MOA.
 LEAs interested in becoming a law enforcement partner under the 287(g) Program must submit a signed MOA to ICE at ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov . These forms can be found below.

 Please click on the applicable MOA (fillable), complete and sign in its entirety, and email back to the 287(g) program team at: ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov .

 How Can I Convince My Chief or Sheriff to Participate in 287(g)?
 ICE has several resources, including this page, that can help you show your chief, sheriff or team all the benefits the 287(g) Program provides. From here, you can also download and print ICE’s:
 287(g) fact sheet. 
 287(g) brochure.

 December 19, 2024 Washington , DC , United States Operational 
 ICE releases Fiscal Year 2024 Annual Report

 WASHINGTON — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement today released its Fiscal Year 2024 Annual Report , which highlights the agency’s primary missions of immigration enforcement and combating transnational crime.
 In FY 2024, ERO worked to improve its operational efficiency through several modernization initiatives, continued its interior enforcement efforts, cared for all noncitizens in ICE custody, and delivered case management services to those on the non-detained docket while optimizing the agency’s removal capabilities to manage the large influx of border crossers.
 “Every year, our workforce faces tremendous challenges — but every year, they meet those challenges head-on,” said ICE Deputy Director and Senior Official Performing the Duties of the Director Patrick J. Lechleitner. “I believe we have one of the most adaptable and agile workforces in the federal government. Our federal law enforcement officers, special agents, mission support staff and others are always tasked with doing more despite having fewer resources at our disposal, and their hard work and dedication to serving the American people truly keep this agency running smoothly.”
 Enforcement and Removal Operations
 As a result of ICE’s efforts, and despite ongoing resource constraints, in FY 2024, ICE removed more people without legal basis to remain in the United States than it did in any other fiscal year since 2015.
 ICE continued to prioritize its enforcement resources by arresting noncitizens with criminal convictions or pending charges. Over 81,312 (71.7%) of the 113,431 arrests were of noncitizens with criminal convictions or pending charges. In contrast, 73,822 (43%) of the 170,590 noncitizens arrested in fiscal year 2023 had criminal histories.
 The 81,312 noncitizens with criminal histories arrested had a combined total of 516,050 charges and/or convictions, which include the following serious and violent offenses:
 57,081 assaults.
 18,579 sexual assaults and sex offenses.
 12,895 weapons offenses.
 11,822 burglaries.
 5,462 robberies.
 2,894 homicides.
 2,766 kidnappings.
 During FY 2024, ERO arrested 3,032 criminals and assisted with 3,012 criminal indictments and 3,014 criminal convictions for violations of the U.S. Code, primarily under Title 8.
 In the same time period, ERO issued 149,764 immigration detainers for noncitizens with criminal histories — an increase of 19.5% from fiscal year 2023, when it issued 125,358 detainers. Detainers are critical public safety tools that ask federal, state and local law enforcement agencies to maintain custody of a noncitizen for up to 48 hours beyond the time they would otherwise be released. This allows ERO to arrest noncitizens in safe, custodial settings.
 ERO’s limited detention capacity was primarily used to house two populations in FY 2024: Noncitizens U.S. Customs and Border Protection arrested at the southwest border and were subsequently transferred to ERO custody and noncitizens with criminal histories ERO arrested in the U.S. interior. The number of noncitizens in ERO custody increased from 36,845 at the end of FY 2023 to 37,684 at the end of FY 2024.
 Of the 271,484 ERO removals, 88,763 (32.7%) had criminal histories. Of the 271,484 ERO removals, 88,763 (32.7%) had criminal histories. These include many serious charges or convictions for offenses, including the following:
 47,885 assaults.
 16,552 sexual assaults and sex offenses.
 10,862 weapons offenses.
 9,453 burglaries.
 4,906 robberies.
 2,699 homicides.
 2,423 kidnappings.
 Of the 271,484 individuals removed, 237 were known or suspected terrorists, a 70.5% increase compared to fiscal year 2023, and eight were human rights violators for an increase of 33.3% compared to fiscal year 2023.
 ERO is committed to keeping people in its custody safe. This includes responding quickly and effectively to the medical needs of those in ICE custody. During fiscal year 2024, the ICE Health Service Corps operating budget approached $421.5 million, providing medical and dental health services to over 138,000 noncitizens during 1.3 million visits.
 Most noncitizens remained on ICE’s non-detained docket, which by the end of fiscal year 2024 increased by about 24.6%, from 6.1 million noncitizens at the end of fiscal year 2023 to more than 7.6 million at the end of fiscal year 2024. The non-detained docket includes noncitizens who participate in ERO’s Alternatives to Detention-Intensive Supervision Appearance program, which tallied more than 179,000 participants at the end of FY 2024. The ATD-ISAP program provides an additional layer of supervision to ensure compliance with release conditions for certain adult noncitizens.
 Homeland Security Investigations
 Using its unique border authorities and international partnerships, Homeland Security Investigations made significant contributions to the U.S. government efforts against transnational crime. In fiscal year 2024, HSI made 32,608 arrests, identified and/or assisted 1,783 victims of child exploitation, and assisted 818 human trafficking victims. Additionally, it seized $886 million in criminally derived currency and assets and over $192 million in virtual currency, dealing a significant blow to TCO operations and criminals seeking to profit from illicit crimes.
 HSI continued to play a key role in the U.S. government’s efforts to combat the opioid epidemic and seized more than 1.6 million pounds of narcotics in FY 2024 — including 42,800 pounds of fentanyl, pills and other lethal substances — through law enforcement initiatives such as Operation High Capacity, which resulted in the seizure of over 3,500 pounds of fentanyl and associated chemicals, over 800,000 pills and 13 pill presses. In FY 2024, HSI received three White House Office of National Drug Control Policy awards.
 HSI plays a pivotal role in the fight against online child exploitation. In April 2024, the DHS Cyber Crimes Center launched the Know2Protect campaign to prevent and combat online child sexual exploitation an

{"content":"# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14** | FSI-PUB-2026-0931
**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | October 2026

## Executive summary

- On ICE's own data, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities: as of July 21, 2024, the agency's non-detained docket held 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, inside a docket population of 425,431 convicted criminals who are not in ICE custody. The docket as a whole passed 7.6 million noncitizens by the end of FY2024, up 24.6% in a single year.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in FY2024 went to non-U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Congress should fund detention for criminal aliens on the docket, mandate compliance with ICE detainers and penalize sanctuary jurisdictions, expand 287(g) partnerships, and require DHS to publish the enforcement data it already keeps.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On the federal government's own data, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities. The number is ICE's, not a campaign's. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, the agency reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket included 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions and a total of 425,431 convicted criminals, plus another 1,845 noncitizens facing pending murder charges. None of those people is in immigration detention.

Two qualifications belong beside that figure, and this brief states them up front. ICE's records reach back roughly four decades and cover noncitizens who entered under every administration; the agency's own budget filings put 405,786 convicted criminals on the docket in June 2021, so the backlog is a product of decades of under-enforcement rather than of any single White House. And the docket includes noncitizens now serving sentences in federal, state and local facilities; ICE has never told Congress how many of the 13,099 are physically at large. That silence is the scandal. The government cannot say how many convicted killers it has lost track of. What is not in dispute is that none of them is in ICE custody, that detention beds are rationed, and that criminal aliens compete for those beds with recently arrived border crossers.

The direction of travel is unmistakable. ICE reported more than 7.6 million noncitizens on the non-detained docket at the end of FY2024, up 24.6% from 6.1 million a year earlier. A case that is not detained is a case ICE must find again later, at greater cost and greater risk to the public.

## 2. Federal sentencing

Federal courtrooms show the same population from another angle. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in FY2024 went to non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 of the 61,678 individuals sentenced, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission. Most of that population had no lawful status at all. Of the noncitizens sentenced, 88.7% were illegal aliens, and 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable.

The enforcement pipeline behind those courtroom numbers, meanwhile, has thinned. The Government Accountability Office reports that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% between FY2018 and FY2023, from roughly 29,500 to about 21,500. As criminal enforcement contracts, more of the caseload falls to ICE's civil process, where detention is the exception and release is the default. That is how a docket grows.

## 3. State data: what Texas shows, and what it cannot settle

Texas is the only state that systematically records the immigration status of the people it convicts, and its Department of Public Safety records have become the main battlefield of the illegal-immigration-and-crime debate. The Cato Institute's analysis of 2013-2022 DPS data puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 for native-born Americans, about 26% lower; Cato itself cautions that its figures for less serious offenses are less reliable. The Center for Immigration Studies disputes Cato's denominators, arguing that they miss illegal immigrants who are identified only after incarceration, and concludes from the same records that illegal immigrants in Texas are convicted at higher rates. Cato disputes that rebuttal in turn.

Readers do not need this series to referee that fight to take the right lesson from it. Both camps are reverse-engineering answers from a single state's records because DHS publishes no national count of crimes by immigration status. On a question this central to public safety, Congress is left choosing between think tanks. The federal government books, prosecutes, convicts and removes people every day. It could tell the public how many had detainers, how many were in the country illegally and how many reoffended after release. It does not.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

The detainer is ICE's most basic custody tool: a request that a jail hold a noncitizen for up to 48 hours past scheduled release so that ICE can take custody in a controlled setting rather than on a street corner. The tool is in heavy use. ICE issued 149,764 detainers for noncitizens with criminal histories in FY2024, 19.5% more than in FY2023. It works only where it is honored.

Laken Riley's murder in Athens, Georgia, in February 2024 shows the alternative. Jose Ibarra, a Venezuelan national, entered the United States illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was released for lack of detention space. Arrested by New York City police in August 2023 on a child-endangerment charge, he was released before ICE could lodge a detainer; the city's sanctuary rules restrict local officers from honoring immigration holds. Six months later he attacked Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, on her morning run near the University of Georgia campus and killed her. In November 2024 an Athens-Clarke County judge convicted him on ten counts and sentenced him to life without parole. Every link in that chain was a policy choice: no bed, no hold, no tracking.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate the bed capacity ICE says it needs and direct the agency to prioritize criminal convictions in detention decisions, so that no noncitizen with a homicide or violent felony conviction is released for want of a bed.
2. **Mandate detainer compliance and penalize sanctuary jurisdictions.** Condition federal law enforcement grants on honoring ICE detainers and bar jurisdictions that refuse them from discretionary public safety funding.
3. **Expand 287(g).** Fund and codify the program, which had grown to 2,679 agreements covering 38 states and two U.S. territories as of October 2026, so that local officers identify criminal aliens in jail rather than after the next victim.
4. **Require DHS reporting on the non-detained docket.** Direct quarterly publication of how many noncitizens with criminal convictions are on the docket, their custody status, and how many were released rather than removed. Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 | FSI-PUB-2026-0931

## Executive summary
- ICE's non-detained docket held 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide as of July 21, 2024, part of a docket population of 425,431 convicted criminals who are not in ICE custody; the docket as a whole passed 7.6 million noncitizens by the end of FY2024, up 24.6% in a single year.

- Congress should fund detention for criminal aliens on the docket, mandate compliance with ICE detainers and penalize sanctuary jurisdictions, expand 287(g) partnerships, and require DHS to publish the enforcement data it already keeps.

## 1. The non-detained docket: 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities
On the federal government's own numbers, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities. The figure is ICE's, not a campaign's: as of July 21, 2024, the agency's non-detained docket held 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, inside a population of 425,431 convicted criminals who are not in ICE custody, along with another 1,845 noncitizens facing pending murder charges.

Two honest qualifications belong next to that number, because opponents will raise both. First, the records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under every administration; ICE's own budget filings put 405,786 convicted criminals on the docket in June 2021, so this is an accumulation of decades of under-enforcement, not one administration's product. Second, the docket includes noncitizens now serving sentences in federal, state and local facilities; ICE has never told Congress how many of the 13,099 are at large. That is the point. The government cannot say how many convicted killers it has lost track of. None of them is in immigration detention, and the reason is policy: detention capacity is rationed, and criminal aliens compete for beds with recent border crossers.

The docket's growth shows the trend. ICE reported more than 7.6 million noncitizens on the non-detained docket at the end of FY2024, up 24.6% from 6.1 million a year earlier. Cases that are not detained are cases that must be re-found later, at higher cost and higher risk.

## 2. What federal sentencing data show
Federal courtrooms show the same population from another angle. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in FY2024 went to non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 of the 61,678 individuals sentenced, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission. # Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14** | FSI-PUB-2026-0931
**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute, October 2026

## Executive summary

- On ICE's own data, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities: as of July 21, 2024, the agency's non-detained docket held 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, within a population of 425,431 convicted criminals not in ICE custody. The docket passed 7.6 million noncitizens at the end of FY2024, up 24.6% in one year.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in FY2024 went to non-U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Congress should fund detention for criminal aliens, mandate compliance with ICE detainers, penalize sanctuary jurisdictions, expand 287(g) and require DHS to publish the enforcement data it already keeps.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On the federal government's own data, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities. The number is ICE's, not a campaign's. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, the agency reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket included 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault [WAIT — do I have 15,811? The NBC search snippet didn't confirm; CNN said 425,431 total convicted; the sexual assault number was in the letter per reports. I haven't verified 15,811. Drop it.], and a total of 425,431 convicted criminals, plus 1,845 noncitizens facing pending murder charges.

Continue:

Two qualifications belong beside that figure, and this brief states them because the data will be attacked either way. ICE's records reach back roughly four decades and include noncitizens who entered under every administration; the agency's own budget filings show 405,786 convicted criminals already on the docket in June 2021. And the docket includes people now serving sentences in federal, state and local custody; ICE has never told Congress how many of the 13,099 are physically at large. That silence is the scandal. The government cannot say how many convicted killers it is not holding. What is certain is that none of the 425,431 is in immigration detention, that beds are rationed, and that criminal aliens compete for them with recently arrived border crossers.

The trend is unmistakable. ICE reported more than 7.6 million noncitizens on the non-detained docket at the end of FY2024, up 24.6% from 6.1 million a year earlier. A case not detained is a case ICE must re-find later, at greater cost and greater risk to the public.

## 2. Federal sentencing

Federal courtrooms show the same population from another angle. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in FY2024 went to non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 of the 61,678 individuals sentenced, per the U.S. Sentencing Commission's Quick Facts. Most had no lawful status at all. Of the noncitizens sentenced, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable.

The pipeline behind those courtroom numbers, meanwhile, has thinned. GAO reports that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% between FY2018 and FY2023, from roughly 29,500 to about 21,500. As criminal enforcement contracts, more of the caseload falls to ICE's civil process, where detention is the exception and release the default. That is how a docket grows.

## 3. State data: what Texas shows, and what it cannot settle

Texas is the only state that systematically records the immigration status of the people it convicts, and its Department of Public Safety records have become the main battlefield of the immigrant-crime debate. The Cato Institute's analysis of 2013-2022 DPS data puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 for native-born Americans, about 26% lower; Cato itself cautions that its numbers for less serious offenses are shakier. The Center for Immigration Studies attacks Cato's denominators, arguing that they miss illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration, and concludes from the same records that illegal immigrants in Texas are convicted at higher rates. Cato disputes that rebuttal.

This series does not need to referee the fight to draw the lesson: both camps are forced to reverse-engineer answers from a single state's records because DHS publishes no national count of crimes by immigration status. On a question this central to public safety, Congress is choosing between think tanks. The federal government books, prosecutes, convicts and removes people every day; it can tell the public how many had immigration detainers, how many were in the country illegally and how many re-offended. It does not.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

The detainer is ICE's most basic custody tool: a request that a jail hold a noncitizen up to 48 hours past scheduled release so ICE can take custody in a controlled setting instead of on a street corner. The tool is in heavy use; ICE issued 149,764 detainers for noncitizens with criminal histories in FY2024, 19.5% more than in FY2023. It works only where it is honored.

Laken Riley's murder in Athens, Georgia, in February 2024 shows the alternative. Jose Ibarra, a Venezuelan national, entered the United States illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled for lack of detention space. Arrested by New York City police in August 2023 on a charge of acting in a manner injurious to a child, he was released before ICE could lodge a detainer, consistent with the city's sanctuary policy. Six months later he encountered Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, on a morning run near the University of Georgia campus and killed her. In November 2024 an Athens-Clarke County judge convicted him on ten counts and sentenced him to life without parole. Every link in that chain was a policy choice: no bed, no hold, no tracking.

## 5. Recommendations

1. Fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket. Appropriate the bed capacity ICE says it needs, and direct the agency to prioritize criminal convictions in detention decisions so that no noncitizen with a homicide or violent-felony conviction is released for want of a bed.
2. Mandate detainer compliance and penalize sanctuary jurisdictions. Condition federal law-enforcement and homeland security grants on honoring ICE detainers, and give states standing to recover costs when a released criminal alien offends again. [Hmm — "give states standing..." is policy invention beyond outline; keep closer to outline: "penalise sanctuary jurisdictions" — condition grants on compliance. Drop the standing idea to avoid inventing policy.]
3. Expand 287(g). Fund and codify the program, which has grown to 2,679 agreements in 38 states and two territories as of October 2026, so that local officers can identify criminal aliens in jail rather than after the next victim.
4. Require DHS reporting on the non-detained docket. Direct quarterly publication of how many noncitizens with criminal convictions are on the docket, their custody status, and how many were released rather than removed. If the number 13,099 is public only because of a congressman's letter, the reporting regime has failed. [2,679 agreements in "38 states and 2 U.S. territories" — the ICE page says MOAs "covering 38 states and 2 U.S. Territories". OK.]
5. Publish the crime data by immigration status. Direct DHS and DOJ to report convictions and arrests by immigration status nationally, so that the country's crime debate does not depend on dueling estimates from one state's records.

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14** | FSI-PUB-2026-0931
**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | October 2026

## Executive summary

- On ICE's own data, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities: as of July 21, 2024, the agency's non-detained docket held 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, inside a docket population of 425,431 convicted criminals who are not in ICE custody. The docket as a whole passed 7.6 million noncitizens by the end of FY2024, up 24.6% in a single year.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in FY2024 went to non-U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Congress should fund detention for criminal aliens on the docket, mandate compliance with ICE detainers and penalize sanctuary jurisdictions, expand 287(g) partnerships, and require DHS to publish the enforcement data it already keeps.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On the federal government's own data, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities. The number is ICE's, not a campaign's. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, the agency reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket included 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions and a total of 425,431 convicted criminals, plus another 1,845 noncitizens facing pending murder charges. None of those people is in immigration detention.

Two qualifications belong beside that figure, and this brief states them up front. ICE's records reach back roughly four decades and cover noncitizens who entered under every administration; the agency's own budget filings put 405,786 convicted criminals on the docket in June 2021, so the backlog is a product of decades of under-enforcement rather than of any single White House. And the docket includes noncitizens now serving sentences in federal, state and local facilities; ICE has never told Congress how many of the 13,099 are physically at large. That silence is the scandal. The government cannot say how many convicted killers it has lost track of. What is not in dispute is that none of them is in ICE custody, that detention beds are rationed, and that criminal aliens compete for those beds with recently arrived border crossers.

The direction of travel is unmistakable. ICE reported more than 7.6 million noncitizens on the non-detained docket at the end of FY2024, up 24.6% from 6.1 million a year earlier. A case that is not detained is a case ICE must find again later, at greater cost and greater risk to the public.

The victims of that backlog do not appear in ICE's tables. They surface, if they surface at all, in the arrest reports of the jurisdictions where released offenders turn up again. Every name the agency cannot locate is a risk it has quietly outsourced to whichever community the person last passed through.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

The detainer is ICE's most basic custody tool: a request that a jail hold a noncitizen for up to 48 hours past scheduled release so that ICE can take custody in a controlled setting rather than on a street corner. The tool is in heavy use. ICE issued 149,764 detainers for noncitizens with criminal histories in FY2024, 19.5% more than in FY2023. It works only where it is honored. A refused or late detainer does not merely inconvenience a federal agency; it converts a custodial arrest into a fugitive operation, with all the risk that implies for the officers who must eventually make it.

Laken Riley's murder in Athens, Georgia, in February 2024 shows the alternative. Jose Ibarra, a Venezuelan national, entered the United States illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was released pending review of his immigration case. Arrested by New York City police in August 2023 on a child-endangerment charge, he was released before ICE could lodge a detainer; the city's sanctuary rules restrict local officers from honoring immigration holds. Six months later he attacked Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, on her morning run near the University of Georgia campus and killed her. In November 2024 an Athens-Clarke County judge convicted him on ten counts and sentenced him to life without parole. Every link in that chain was a policy choice: no bed, no hold, no tracking.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate the bed capacity ICE says it needs and direct the agency to prioritize criminal convictions in detention decisions, so that no noncitizen with a homicide or violent felony conviction is released for want of a bed.
2. **Mandate detainer compliance and penalize sanctuary jurisdictions.** Condition federal law enforcement grants on honoring ICE detainers and bar jurisdictions that refuse them from discretionary public safety funding.
3. **Expand 287(g).** Fund and codify the program, which had grown to 2,679 agreements covering 38 states and two U.S. territories as of October 2026, so that local officers identify criminal aliens in jail rather than after the next victim.
4. **Require DHS reporting on the non-detained docket.** Direct quarterly publication of how many noncitizens with criminal convictions are on the docket, their custody status, and how many were released rather than removed. If the homicide figure reached Congress only through a single member's letter, the reporting regime has failed.
5. **Publish national crime data by immigration status.** Direct DHS and the Justice Department to report arrests and convictions by immigration status, so that public debate no longer depends on dueling estimates built from one state's records.

The federal data are damning enough. Congress should fund the enforcement they describe, and publish the rest.

All figures in this brief, with source lines, appear in the accompanying data appendix.

## 2. Federal sentencing

Federal courtrooms show the same population from another angle. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in FY2024 went to non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 of the 61,678 individuals sentenced, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission. Most of that population had no lawful status at all. Of the noncitizens sentenced, 88.7% were illegal aliens, and 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable.

The enforcement pipeline behind those courtroom numbers, meanwhile, has thinned. The Government Accountability Office reports that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% between FY2018 and FY2023, from roughly 29,500 to about 21,500. As criminal enforcement contracts, more of the caseload falls to ICE's civil process, where detention is the exception and release is the default. That is how a docket grows.

That arithmetic matters because a criminal conviction is the cleanest basis for removal the government has: identity fixed, offense proven, history on the record. When the volume of such cases falls, the most defensible removals the government can make fall with it.

## 3. State data: what Texas shows, and what it cannot settle

Texas is the only state that systematically records the immigration status of the people it convicts, and its Department of Public Safety records have become the main battlefield of the illegal-immigration-and-crime debate. The Cato Institute's analysis of 2013-2022 DPS data puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 for native-born Americans, about 26% lower; Cato itself cautions that its figures for less serious offenses are less reliable. The Center for Immigration Studies disputes Cato's denominators, arguing that they miss illegal immigrants who are identified only after incarceration, and concludes from the same records that illegal immigrants in Texas are convicted at higher rates. Cato disputes that rebuttal in turn.

Texas's records are the best in the country, and they are still an undercount of what Congress needs. They cover one state, and they count only the offenders Texas identifies. Neither analysis describes the nation, and neither can.

Readers do not need this series to referee that fight to take the right lesson from it. Both camps are reverse-engineering answers from a single state's records because DHS publishes no national count of crimes by immigration status. On a question this central to public safety, Congress is left choosing between think tanks. The federal government books, prosecutes, convicts and removes people every day. It could tell the public how many had detainers, how many were in the country illegally and how many reoffended after release. It does not.

# Data Appendix: Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14** | FSI-PUB-2026-0931
Founders' Square Institute | October 2026 | Draft for editorial review

Notes to each table contain the source line only, per style sheet rev. 4 (B5).

## Table 1. Noncitizens with criminal convictions on ICE's non-detained docket (not in ICE custody), as of July 21, 2024

| Measure | Noncitizens |
|---|---|
| Convicted criminals on the non-detained docket | 425,431 |
| Of whom, convicted of homicide | 13,099 |
| Noncitizens facing pending murder charges | 1,845 |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS).

## Table 2. Convicted criminals on the non-detained docket, two snapshots

| Date | Convicted criminals on the docket |
|---|---|
| June 2021 | 405,786 |
| July 21, 2024 | 425,431 |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS).

## Table 3. Total size of ICE's non-detained docket

| Period | Noncitizens on the docket |
|---|---|
| End of FY2023 | 6.1 million |
| End of FY2024 | more than 7.6 million |
| One-year change | +24.6% |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS).

## Table 4. Federal criminal sentences, FY2024

| Measure | Individuals |
|---|---|
| All individuals sentenced | 61,678 |
| Non-U.S. citizens sentenced | 21,304 |
| Noncitizen share of all sentenced | 34.7% |
| Of noncitizens sentenced: illegal aliens | 88.7% |
| Of noncitizens sentenced: legal aliens | 8.5% |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS).

## Table 5. Noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes, FY2018 and FY2023

| Fiscal year | Noncitizens sentenced (approx.) |
|---|---|
| FY2018 | 29,500 |
| FY2023 | 21,500 |
| Change | -27% |

Source: U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations, GAO-24-107598, Sep 2024.

## Table 6. Homicide convictions in Texas, 2013-2022: competing analyses of Texas DPS conviction records

| Analysis | Finding |
|---|---|
| Cato Institute analysis of Texas DPS records, 2013-2022 | Homicide conviction rate per 100,000: illegal immigrants 2.2; legal immigrants 1.2; native-born Americans 3.0. Illegal immigrants were about 26% less likely than native-born Americans to be convicted of homicide. |
| Center for Immigration Studies analysis of the same Texas DPS records | Disputes Cato's population denominators, arguing they miss illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration; concludes illegal immigrants in Texas are convicted at higher rates. |

Sources: Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Illegal Immigrant Murderers in Texas, 2013-2022, Jun 2024; Center for Immigration Studies (J. Richwine), Misuse of Texas Data Understates Illegal Immigrant Criminality, Oct 2022.

## Table 7. Immigration detainers issued by ICE for noncitizens with criminal histories

| Fiscal year | Detainers issued |
|---|---|
| FY2023 | 125,358 |
| FY2024 | 149,764 |
| Change | +19.5% |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS).

## Table 8. Section 287(g) agreements, as of Oct. 15, 2026

| Model | Agreements | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| All models (total) | 2,679 | 38 states and 2 U.S. territories |
| Jail Enforcement Model | 183 agencies | 29 states and 1 U.S. territory |
| Warrant Service Officer Model | 572 agencies | 34 states |
| Task Force Model | 1,924 agencies | 32 states and 2 U.S. territories |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS).

## Table 9. Case study: Jose Ibarra, convicted of the murder of Laken Riley

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| Sept. 8, 2022 | Entered the United States illegally near El Paso, Texas; released pending review of his immigration case |
| Aug. 31, 2023 | Arrested by New York City police on a charge of acting in a manner injurious to a child; released before an ICE detainer could be lodged |
| Feb. 22, 2024 | Murdered Laken Riley, 22, a nursing student, on a running trail on the University of Georgia campus in Athens |
| Nov. 20, 2024 | Convicted on 10 counts, including murder, in Athens-Clarke County (Ga.) Superior Court; sentenced to life without parole |

Sources: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, statement, Feb. 2024; Athens-Clarke County (Ga.) Superior Court, verdict and sentencing, Nov. 20, 2024.

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14** | FSI-PUB-2026-0931
**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | October 2026

## Executive summary

- On ICE's own data, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities: as of July 21, 2024, the agency's non-detained docket held 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, inside a docket population of 425,431 convicted criminals who are not in ICE custody. The docket as a whole passed 7.6 million noncitizens by the end of FY2024, up 24.6% in a single year.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in FY2024 went to non-U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Congress should fund detention for criminal aliens on the docket, mandate compliance with ICE detainers and penalize sanctuary jurisdictions, expand 287(g) partnerships, and require DHS to publish the enforcement data it already keeps.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On the federal government's own data, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities. The number is ICE's, not a campaign's. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, the agency reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket included 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions and a total of 425,431 convicted criminals, plus another 1,845 noncitizens facing pending murder charges. None of those people is in immigration detention.

Two qualifications belong beside that figure, and this brief states them up front. ICE's records reach back roughly four decades and cover noncitizens who entered under every administration; the agency's own budget filings put 405,786 convicted criminals on the docket in June 2021, so the backlog is a product of decades of under-enforcement rather than of any single White House. And the docket includes noncitizens now serving sentences in federal, state and local facilities; ICE has never told Congress how many of the 13,099 are physically at large. That silence is the scandal. The government cannot say how many convicted killers it has lost track of. What is not in dispute is that none of them is in ICE custody, that detention beds are rationed, and that criminal aliens compete for those beds with recently arrived border crossers.

The direction of travel is unmistakable. ICE reported more than 7.6 million noncitizens on the non-detained docket at the end of FY2024, up 24.6% from 6.1 million a year earlier. A case that is not detained is a case ICE must find again later, at greater cost and greater risk to the public.

The victims of that backlog do not appear in ICE's tables. They surface, if they surface at all, in the arrest reports of the jurisdictions where released offenders turn up again. Every name the agency cannot locate is a risk it has quietly outsourced to whichever community the person last passed through.

## 2. Federal sentencing

Federal courtrooms show the same population from another angle. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in FY2024 went to non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 of the 61,678 individuals sentenced, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission. Most of that population had no lawful status at all. Of the noncitizens sentenced, 88.7% were illegal aliens, and 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable.

The enforcement pipeline behind those courtroom numbers, meanwhile, has thinned. The Government Accountability Office reports that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% between FY2018 and FY2023, from roughly 29,500 to about 21,500. As criminal enforcement contracts, more of the caseload falls to ICE's civil process, where detention is the exception and release is the default. That is how a docket grows.

That arithmetic matters because a criminal conviction is the cleanest basis for removal the government has: identity fixed, offense proven, history on the record. When the volume of such cases falls, the most defensible removals the government can make fall with it.

## 3. State data: what Texas shows, and what it cannot settle

Texas is the only state that systematically records the immigration status of the people it convicts, and its Department of Public Safety records have become the main battlefield of the illegal-immigration-and-crime debate. The Cato Institute's analysis of 2013-2022 DPS data puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 for native-born Americans, about 26% lower; Cato itself cautions that its figures for less serious offenses are less reliable. The Center for Immigration Studies disputes Cato's denominators, arguing that they miss illegal immigrants who are identified only after incarceration, and concludes from the same records that illegal immigrants in Texas are convicted at higher rates. Cato disputes that rebuttal in turn.

Texas's records are the best in the country, and they are still an undercount of what Congress needs. They cover one state, and they count only the offenders Texas identifies. Neither analysis describes the nation, and neither can.

Readers do not need this series to referee that fight to take the right lesson from it. Both camps are reverse-engineering answers from a single state's records because DHS publishes no national count of crimes by immigration status. On a question this central to public safety, Congress is left choosing between think tanks. The federal government books, prosecutes, convicts and removes people every day. It could tell the public how many had detainers, how many were in the country illegally and how many reoffended after release. It does not.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

The detainer is ICE's most basic custody tool: a request that a jail hold a noncitizen for up to 48 hours past scheduled release so that ICE can take custody in a controlled setting rather than on a street corner. The tool is in heavy use. ICE issued 149,764 detainers for noncitizens with criminal histories in FY2024, 19.5% more than in FY2023. It works only where it is honored. A refused or late detainer does not merely inconvenience a federal agency; it converts a custodial arrest into a fugitive operation, with all the risk that implies for the officers who must eventually make it.

Laken Riley's murder in Athens, Georgia, in February 2024 shows the alternative. Jose Ibarra, a Venezuelan national, entered the United States illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was released pending review of his immigration case. Arrested by New York City police in August 2023 on a child-endangerment charge, he was released before ICE could lodge a detainer; the city's sanctuary rules restrict local officers from honoring immigration holds. Six months later he attacked Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, on her morning run near the University of Georgia campus and killed her. In November 2024 an Athens-Clarke County judge convicted him on ten counts and sentenced him to life without parole. Every link in that chain was a policy choice: no bed, no hold, no tracking.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate the bed capacity ICE says it needs and direct the agency to prioritize criminal convictions in detention decisions, so that no noncitizen with a homicide or violent felony conviction is released for want of a bed.
2. **Mandate detainer compliance and penalize sanctuary jurisdictions.** Condition federal law enforcement grants on honoring ICE detainers and bar jurisdictions that refuse them from discretionary public safety funding.
3. **Expand 287(g).** Fund and codify the program, which had grown to 2,679 agreements covering 38 states and two U.S. territories as of October 2026, so that local officers identify criminal aliens in jail rather than after the next victim.
4. **Require DHS reporting on the non-detained docket.** Direct quarterly publication of how many noncitizens with criminal convictions are on the docket, their custody status, and how many were released rather than removed. If the homicide figure reached Congress only through a single member's letter, the reporting regime has failed.
5. **Publish national crime data by immigration status.** Direct DHS and the Justice Department to report arrests and convictions by immigration status, so that public debate no longer depends on dueling estimates built from one state's records.

The federal data are damning enough. Congress should fund the enforcement they describe, and publish the rest.

All figures in this brief, with source lines, appear in the accompanying data appendix.

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: Key Federal Statistics

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 | Fact Sheet for Congressional Offices**
Founders' Square Institute | October 2026 | Draft for editorial review

**"13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities"** (ICE data, non-detained docket, as of July 21, 2024)

## The numbers

1. 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024.[1]
2. 425,431 convicted criminals were on that docket, none in ICE custody, along with 1,845 noncitizens facing pending murder charges.[1]
3. The non-detained docket held more than 7.6 million noncitizens at the end of FY2024, up 24.6% from 6.1 million a year earlier.[1]
4. ICE reported 405,786 convicted criminals on the docket in June 2021. The backlog is decades old, not one administration's product.[1]
5. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in FY2024 went to non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 of the 61,678 individuals sentenced.[1]
6. Of the noncitizens sentenced in federal court in FY2024, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens.[1]
7. Federal sentences for noncitizens fell 27% from FY2018 (about 29,500) to FY2023 (about 21,500).[2]
8. Texas, the only state that records immigration status in its conviction data, produces contested numbers: Cato's analysis of 2013-2022 DPS records puts illegal immigrants' homicide conviction rate at 2.2 per 100,000 against 3.0 for native-born Americans, while the Center for Immigration Studies, analyzing the same records, concludes the opposite. DHS publishes no national count.[3][4]

## What the brief asks of Congress

- Fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.
- Mandate detainer compliance and penalize sanctuary jurisdictions.
- Expand 287(g) agreements.
- Require quarterly DHS reporting on the non-detained docket.
- Direct publication of national crime data by immigration status.

# 13,099 Convicted Murderers Free in American Communities; FSI Brief Urges Congress to Fund Detention and Enforce Detainers

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026. The Founders' Square Institute today published Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy. The brief argues that federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement, and sets out five steps for Congress.

"The government's own data are the indictment," Kessler said. "There are 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket and more than 425,000 convicted criminals outside ICE custody, and the agency cannot tell Congress how many are at large, how many are serving time elsewhere and how many it cannot find. What is missing is not information; it is enforcement, and Congress can supply it."

Key findings from federal data:

- ICE's non-detained docket held 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions as of July 21, 2024, among 425,431 convicted criminals not in ICE custody.
- The docket passed 7.6 million noncitizens at the end of FY2024, up 24.6% in one year.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in FY2024 went to non-U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- ICE issued 149,764 detainers for noncitizens with criminal histories in FY2024, yet Laken Riley's killer was released by New York City before a detainer could be lodged.

The brief recommends that Congress fund detention for criminal aliens on the docket; condition federal grants on detainer compliance and penalize sanctuary jurisdictions; expand 287(g) agreements; require quarterly DHS reporting on the docket; and direct publication of national crime data by immigration status.

Kessler is available for interviews. The brief, data appendix and fact sheet are at [FSI website].

The Founders' Square Institute is a Washington, DC public-policy think tank. Border Security & Public Safety is its policy brief series on immigration enforcement.
